item.title: PM: Protect water bodies, ensure sustainable fisheries
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Sunday called for greater public awareness and coordinated efforts to save rivers, canals, haors, beels and other water bodies from pollution, saying safeguarding the environment is essential to protecting the country’s fisheries resources.
“If we are truly conscious and want to protect our environment, and if we want to save our fish, then we must also pay attention to protecting the environment. We must safeguard our natural environment,” he said, pointing to the growing pollution of water bodies by plastic bottles, tissue paper and other waste.
The prime minister made the remarks while inaugurating National Fisheries Fortnight-2026 at the George Institute Mini Stadium in Achmita union of Katiadi upazila.
The fortnight is being observed across the country from Sunday to August 30 under the theme “A self-sufficient country through silver fish, Bangladesh first.”
Tarique Rahman said fisheries play a vital role in meeting the country’s nutritional needs while creating employment through fish farming, catching, transportation, processing and marketing.
“There is a very important issue closely linked to fisheries that is the environment. For whatever reason, we are seeing that the environment of our canals, rivers, haors, beels and other water bodies is gradually being degraded by various forms of waste generated by our daily activities, including tissue paper, plastics and discarded water bottles,” he said.
The prime minister said protecting the environment will enable people to live in a healthy environment, allow children to grow up in healthy surroundings, and help the country develop its fisheries and livestock sectors sustainably.
He urged everyone to work together to conserve aquatic resources, promote environment-friendly and sustainable fish farming and distribution, and increase fish production, harvesting and productivity so that Bangladesh can become a nutritious, self-reliant and prosperous country.
“To build such a Bangladesh, all of us must work with awareness, sincerity and dedication,” Tarique Rahman said.
He also called for the restoration and productive use of the country’s ponds, haors, beels and other water bodies to expand fish production, create employment and raise incomes, particularly among young people and marginalised communities.
“Bangladesh is a riverine country. There are opportunities to become self-reliant by using ponds, beels, haors, baors and other water bodies, or even small areas of land, for fish farming,” the prime minister said.
At the inaugural program, Tarique Rahman handed over the National Fisheries Medal (Gold Medal) to 14 individuals and organisations in 13 categories in recognition of their contributions to fisheries production, innovation, research, technology, conservation, exports and employment generation.
Highlighting the importance of the fisheries sector, he said it plays a vital role in increasing the incomes of marginalized people.
The prime minister said the government has decided to renovate unused water bodies across the country, release fish fry there and allocate those to local young people so that they can engage in fish farming and create employment.
He said he has already instructed State Minister for Fisheries and Livestock Sultan Salauddin Tuku to take necessary steps in this regard.
Tarique Rahman said Bangladesh earned more than Tk6,000 crore in foreign currency by exporting fish and fish products to around 52 countries in the 2025-26 fiscal year.
He credited entrepreneurs, traders, fish farmers and everyone involved in the sector with the achievement.
The prime minister said Bangladesh has significant potential to emerge as a major global producer of freshwater fish.
Citing a report published by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) in June, he said Bangladesh ranked fifth globally in the production of aquatic animals, including fish, while it ranked second in the world in inland fish capture.
Tarique Rahman said planned efforts could create more employment in the fisheries sector while increasing foreign exchange earnings.
Referring to ongoing initiatives, he said the Department of Fisheries has formed 300 clusters in the Khulna region to promote cluster-based shrimp farming, resulting in more than doubling average production in around 7,500 farms.
The prime minister also said a master plan has been prepared to develop shrimp farming on around 7,000 acres of land in Chakaria upazila of Cox's Bazar, including infrastructure development.
He also highlighted government measures for the conservation and development of hilsa, describing it as not only Bangladesh's national fish and an economic asset but also a globally recognized Geographical Indication (GI) product.
Tarique Rahman said Ilish accounts for around 10% of the country's total fish production and more than 1% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
The government is also giving priority to the fisheries, livestock and aquatic-resource sectors because millions of Bangladeshis depend directly or indirectly on these activities, he said.
The prime minister said around 20 million people, including 1.4 million women, are directly or indirectly dependent on the fisheries sector.
For this reason, he said the government considers ensuring the safety and uninterrupted development of the sector a major responsibility.
Tarique Rahman said fisheries, livestock and the blue economy have been placed among the government's priority sectors because millions of Bangladeshis remain connected to these activities as part of the country's traditional economic structure.
He said the government is committed to improving the livelihoods of fish farmers and fishermen.
The prime minister said fish farmers will be brought under the Farmers’ Card program, while registration and issuance of identity cards for fishermen are ongoing.
For the first time in the 2026-27 fiscal year, fishermen in the Sundarbans and haor regions have also been brought under the VGF program during fishing bans, he said.
Tarique Rahman also called on entrepreneurs and businesses to explore new overseas markets for Bangladeshi products.
He said Bangladesh has exported hatching eggs to Nigeria for the first time in June and urged entrepreneurs to seek new export opportunities, assuring them of government support.
The prime minister also announced that the government has established a Tk500 crore startup fund to encourage technology-driven employment, research, innovation and the development of a knowledge-based economy.
He said promising startups will receive grants ranging from Tk5 lakh to Tk5 crore, stressing that the assistance will be provided as grants, not loans.
Tarique Rahman urged young entrepreneurs to take advantage of the opportunity.
National Fisheries Fortnight will feature rallies, discussions, seminars, fish fairs, fish-fry releases, technology exhibitions, awareness campaigns and programs to honour successful fish farmers across the country.
The programs aim to promote safe fish production, sustainable management of fisheries resources, modern farming technologies and awareness of the nutritional value of fish.
Fisheries and Livestock Minister Mohammed Aminur Rashid chaired the inaugural program.
State Minister Tuku, State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives Mir Shahe Alam, State Minister for Textiles and Jute Md Shariful Alam, Kishoreganj-2 MP Md Jalal Uddin, Fisheries and Livestock Secretary Delwar Hossain and Department of Fisheries Director General Md Khaled Kanak, among others, attended the event.
Earlier in the day, the prime minister released fish fry into the old Brahmaputra River in Pakundia, visited the Katiadi Carp Hatchery Complex and exchanged greetings with local people.
Following the fisheries program, he is scheduled to inaugurate a tree-planting program at Sholakia Eidgah and attend a Family Card distribution program at Kishoreganj Stadium.

item.title: Bangladeshis hold more favorable view of India than vice versa
item.description:
A recent opinion survey reveals that Bangladeshis hold a significantly more positive view of India than Indians do of Bangladesh.
While 42% of Bangladeshi adults view India favorably, only 25% of Indian adults share a positive view of Bangladesh, according to Washington-based organization, the Pew Research Center.
Despite this gap, favorable ratings in both neighboring nations have dropped over the last two years.
In 2024, India's favorability in Bangladesh stood at 57%, while Bangladesh's favorability in India was 35%.
While the drops are mutual, a greater percentage of Bangladeshis continue to hold favorable views on India than Indian’s viewing Bangladesh positively.
The survey, conducted from February 8 to May 7, 2026, across Bangladesh, India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, examined how people in the four countries view one another.
The survey interviewed 1,044 people in Bangladesh, 3,566 in India, 1,039 in Pakistan and 2,513 in Sri Lanka.
Most adults in Pakistan (66%) and Sri Lanka (56%) have positive views of Bangladesh, while a quarter of Indian adults hold this view.
Many people express a favorable view of Pakistan in Sri Lanka (57%) and Bangladesh (54%), while very few in India do the same (8%).
When asked what country poses the greatest threat to their own, Indians also most often name Pakistan.
Sri Lanka is the only South Asian country Pew asked about viewed more favorably than unfavorably in the three others surveyed. Around half of adults in each of the other nations see Sri Lanka positively, while a third or fewer see it negatively.
Of the four countries Pew asked about, India has the broadest range in favorability. An overwhelming majority of Sri Lankans express a positive view of India, compared with 42% of Bangladeshis and 7% of Pakistanis.

item.title: Bangladesh wants ‘conducive environment’ before PM’s India visit
item.description:
Bangladesh wants a “conducive environment” created before Prime Minister Tarique Rahman visits India, including the extradition of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, who is currently in India after being sentenced to death for crimes against humanity.
Dhaka has also sought the extradition of suspects accused of killing Inqilab Mancha spokesperson Sharif Osman Hadi under the bilateral extradition treaty.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson AKM Shahidul Karim conveyed the government’s position at a media briefing at the ministry on Sunday.
He said officials from Bangladesh and India had been in discussions for several weeks over Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s proposed bilateral visit, but the process was disrupted after Sheikh Hasina was recently allowed to publicly address in Delhi.
“We have made our position clear. We believe a conducive environment needs to be created for the visit,” Shahidul said.
“To this end, we have requested the Indian authorities to take prompt action on our requests for the extradition of Sheikh Hasina and other fugitives,” he added.
He said India should hand over the suspects accused of killing Osman Hadi under the bilateral extradition treaty. “We are waiting for their response,” he said.
The spokesperson said Bangladesh would continue to pursue its “Bangladesh First” policy in developing friendly relations with neighbouring and other countries based on sovereign equality, national dignity, non-interference in each other’s internal affairs and mutual benefit.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has invited Tarique Rahman to attend the outreach session of the BRICS Summit, scheduled to be held in Delhi in September, in his capacity as BIMSTEC chair. India also invited him for a bilateral visit in February.
Uncertainty had emerged over Tarique Rahman’s participation in the BRICS Summit after Sheikh Hasina was allowed to address an event in Delhi. However, diplomatic efforts by Dhaka and New Delhi later revived discussions on the prime minister’s proposed bilateral visit.

item.title: Khasru: Govt seeking alternative financing as banking sector faces serious capital deficit
item.description:
Stating that Bangladesh’s banking sector is suffering from a serious capital deficit caused by massive money laundering, Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury on Sunday said the government is actively seeking alternative financing mechanisms and dedicated investment funds to drive countrywide economic growth.
Speaking as the chief guest at a luncheon discussion titled "Building Investor Confidence: From Policy Reforms to Effective Implementation" hosted by the American Chamber of Commerce in Bangladesh (AmCham) at a city hotel, he emphasized that traditional high-speed banking alone can no longer satisfy the country's investment needs under current constraints.
"There is a serious deficit in the banking sector as a huge amount of money has been laundered out of the country. Depositors are struggling to get their money back, making immediate capitalization essential," Khasru said.
He noted that in response to this structural shortfall, Bangladesh is architecting alternative financial channels and receiving positive responses from foreign countries and international organizations to create dedicated investment funds.
Addressing structural bottlenecks in business and trade, the minister acknowledged that Bangladesh remains an "over-regulated" country where existing government regulations and regulatory systems are not functioning effectively.
He also outlined several reform initiatives undertaken by the government.
Khasru said the National Board of Revenue (NBR) is undergoing structural division to separate its policy-making functions from tax execution.
Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury speaks at a luncheon discussion titled `Building Investor Confidence: From Policy Reforms to Effective Implementation` at a city hotel on Sunday, August 16, 2026. Photo: UNB
The government plans to fully automate investor services, tax processing, and customs logistics to create a hassle-free, business-friendly environment, he said.
The minister said the primary allocation in the national budget will be dedicated to implementing comprehensive structural reforms.
He said Bangladesh is pivoting towards advanced Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) management to enhance administrative efficiency.
Addressing questions regarding energy shortages, Khasru asserted that overcoming the energy crisis requires a long-term strategic approach rather than short-term stopgap solutions.
Opening the discussion, AmCham President Syed Mohammad Kamal highlighted that business community members are prioritizing energy security, stable and predictable tax structures, business-friendly policies, and overarching macroeconomic stability.
Echoing positive prospects for investors, HSBC Bangladesh Chief Executive Officer Mahbubur Rahman noted that Bangladesh possesses the essential ingredients to attract foreign investment, citing a market of 18 crore people, a flourishing export sector, and growing remittance inflows that help maintain currency and foreign exchange stability.
The high-level AmCham event brought together prominent businessmen, economists, senior government officials, foreign trade delegates, and AmCham members operating in Bangladesh.

item.title: Minister: Access to justice means ensuring human rights
item.description:
Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Md Asaduzzaman has said access to justice means ensuring human rights.
“Every citizen has inalienable, inherent and universal rights, and the state has a responsibility to ensure that citizens can access justice and exercise those rights,” he said while speaking as the chief guest at the opening session of a two-day coordination meeting that concluded on Sunday.
The minister also highlighted the importance of digitalization, stronger public awareness of legal rights and legal aid services, greater institutional engagement by the Directorate of Bangladesh Legal Aid, and recognition of high-performing legal aid and judicial officers. “We are committed to reducing the backlog of cases within one year,” he said.
Bangladesh is advancing efforts to make the government’s legal aid services more accessible and efficient through digitalization, said a media release issued by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) on Sunday.
The two-day coordination meeting brought justice sector stakeholders together at BRAC-CDM, Gazipur, to support the rollout of the new Digital Legal Aid System under the “Accelerating Digital Legal Aid Services in Bangladesh” project.
The meeting ended on Sunday with District and Sessions Judges from the eight districts discussing Online Dispute Resolution, committee activation, training, and legal aid data management, with particular attention to improving access for women, persons with disabilities and people living in poverty.
Implemented by the DBLA under the ministry with financial support from the European Union and support from the UNDP, the project aims to modernize legal aid delivery.
The new system is expected to simplify legal aid applications, case tracking, lawyer assignment, mediation, notifications and data management.
The event brought together judges and legal aid officials to strengthen local legal aid mechanisms, advance digital service delivery and make justice more accessible to underserved communities.
The initiative will focus on activating Upazila and Union Legal Aid Committees, improving digital case management and promoting online dispute resolution across Rajbari, Habiganj, Barguna, Netrokona, Joypurhat, Thakurgaon, Jhenaidah and Khagrachhari.
A key focus of the meeting is the selection and functionalisation of 45 Upazila Legal Aid Committees and 300 Union Legal Aid Committees across the eight districts.
These committees are expected to bring legal aid services closer to communities, particularly for people who face financial, geographic or social barriers in accessing formal justice institutions.
The opening session was also attended by Law and Justice Division Secretary Liaquat Ali Molla, DBLA Director General Md Monjurul Hossain, Chargé d’Affaires of the European Union Delegation to Bangladesh Baiba Zarina and Senior Rule of Law, Justice and Security Adviser at UNDP Bangladesh Romana Schweiger.

item.title: Info minister: Govt to establish Modern Information Complex in every district, upazila
item.description:
Information and Broadcasting Minister Zahir Uddin Swapon has said the government is constructing modern information complex in every division.
The program will also be expanded at district and upazila level, he said while inaugurating the construction work of the modern Barisal Divisional Information Complex at Ichhakathi in Kashipur of Barisal city on Sunday.
The event was organized by the Department of Mass Communication under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.
The information complexes will multifaceted centers for information, knowledge, entertainment and research, he said.
“The complexes will not only be eye-catching buildings; they will serve as hubs of information, knowledge and research. The complexes will primarily function as Digital Information Service Centers, providing a wide range of digital services to the public,” he said.
Swapon said development work under the project is already underway in 26 districts. To popularize the facilities and encourage students to engage in research, promotional leaflets will be distributed to local educational institutions through the ministry, he said.
“The government’s objective is not limited to infrastructure development; rather, it aims to bring the quality of the complexes up to international standard,” he said.
To achieve this, Swapon said, both infrastructure engineering and software engineering are being given separate and equal importance.
Highlighting the technological facilities planned for the complexes, Swapon said they would feature state-of-the-art, technology-enabled cineplexes and electronic screens, with facilities for screening digital movies as well as 3D and 4D films.
Speaking as chair of the event, Secretary of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting Mahbuba Farjana said the information complexes would play important role in combating misinformation and disinformation.
Barisal Divisional Commissioner Khalil Ahmed, Barisal City Corporation Administrator Advocate Bilkis Akter Jahan Shirin, spoke among others on the occasion.
In his welcome address, Project Director Moniruzzaman said the seven-storey modern Information Complex in Barisal is being constructed at a cost of Taka 17.63 crore.
Later, Deputy Project Director Rezaur Rabbi Moni presented details of the project through a multimedia presentation.

item.title: Model Ridhika Ridhi’s boyfriend sent to jail in suicide abetment case
item.description:
Model Ridhika Ridhi’s boyfriend, Hasibur Rahman, has been sent to jail in a case filed over her death at her Bashundhara Residential Area home in Dhaka. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Mahbub Alam passed the order on Sunday, said Prosecution Department Sub-Inspector Kamal Hossain.
Family members found Ridhi hanging from a ceiling fan in her bedroom on Saturday morning. She was rushed to Kurmitola General Hospital where doctors declared her dead.
Ridhi’s mother Moni Begum filed a case on the same day, accusing Hasibur of abetting her daughter’s suicide.
Hasibur, who had visited Ridhi’s home that day, was arrested from the spot.
On Sunday, Vatara police Sub-Inspector Abdul Wadud, the investigating officer, produced Hasibur before the court and sought his detention in jail.
In the petition, police said preliminary interrogation and investigation had yielded sufficient evidence supporting the allegations against Hasibur. They said he had confessed to the offence and admitted his involvement during questioning.
Police also expressed concern that he might flee if released on bail.
Hasibur’s lawyer, Golam Kibria Choton, sought bail and requested a hearing on Tuesday. The court sent Hasibur to jail and fixed Tuesday for the bail hearing. Police said Ridhi had been on a video call with Hasibur when the incident occurred. Although the death initially appeared to be a suicide, investigators are probing the circumstances to determine the exact cause of death.
Ridhi, who worked as a model, also acted in several dramas, including Ekhane Manush Bikri Hoy, Bahurupi, Double Honeymoon and Sundori.

item.title: 10 dating trends taking over 2026 — and what they say about modern love
item.description:
Dating has never stayed still for long. From supervised courtship to casual dates and, eventually, dating apps, the way people meet and build relationships has changed with society.
In 2026, that shift is becoming even more noticeable. While dating apps remain a major part of modern romance, many singles are becoming more intentional about who they date, what they want, and how much time they are willing to invest in relationships.
Here are 10 trends shaping modern dating this year.
Politics is increasingly becoming part of the dating conversation. For some singles, particularly younger people, political beliefs can reveal how a potential partner views issues such as gender, equality, religion, and social responsibility.
As a result, political compatibility is becoming an important consideration before a relationship gets serious. For some, a major ideological difference is no longer something they are willing to overlook.
Terms once largely associated with therapy have become part of everyday relationship conversations.
People now casually talk about having an “anxious attachment style,” needing to protect their “nervous system” or setting boundaries. Used appropriately, this language can help people communicate emotional needs and recognize patterns in their relationships.
However, experts caution against turning psychological terms into labels. Words such as “narcissist” and “trauma bond” can lose their meaning when they are used casually or incorrectly.
The days of trying to decode vague messages and uncertain intentions may be fading.
“Clear coding” refers to being direct about what someone wants from dating, whether that means a serious relationship, casual dating, or simply getting to know someone. The approach can reduce misunderstandings and make it easier for people to identify compatibility early.
For singles tired of situationships and mixed signals, honesty is becoming part of the attraction.
A first date no longer has to mean an elaborate dinner followed by an evening of activities.
Microdating involves short, low-pressure meetings such as a 30-minute coffee or a quick walk. The idea is simple: meet someone in person, see whether there is a connection, and decide whether it is worth investing more time.
The approach can also make dating less expensive and reduce the pressure often associated with a traditional first date.
Sometimes, the most influential person in your dating life is not the person you are dating — it is your friend.
Friendfluence describes the growing role friends play in choosing or evaluating romantic partners. From analyzing screenshots in group chats to offering opinions after a first date, friends can have a significant influence on whether someone gets a second chance.
For many singles, the group chat has effectively become part of the dating process.
After years of swiping, some singles are turning away from dating apps in search of more organic connections.
Concerns about fake profiles, catfishing, endless conversations, and dating-app fatigue have encouraged some people to meet potential partners through friends, social events, workplaces, hobbies, and other real-world settings.
Dating apps are not disappearing, but the desire to meet people offline is becoming more visible.
Some couples are choosing to keep their relationships private until they are certain about their future together.
Instead of immediately posting a new partner online, people are increasingly waiting until an engagement or another major milestone before making the relationship public.
The trend reflects a broader shift toward separating private relationships from social media performance.
Long-term relationships can easily become routine, particularly when work and other responsibilities take over everyday life.
The “777 rule” offers a simple framework for maintaining connection: a date night every 7 days, a weekend away every 7 weeks, and a vacation every 7 months.
The idea is less about following the numbers perfectly and more about making intentional time for a partner.
Not every dating trend is necessarily healthy.
“Shrekking,” inspired by the animated film Shrek , refers to dating someone perceived as being less conventionally attractive or desirable in the belief that they will offer better treatment or give one person greater control in the relationship.
The strategy can easily backfire, particularly when a relationship is built around assumptions about someone’s appearance, status, or perceived “league.”
Social media has changed what people can gain from relationships.
“Throning” describes dating someone primarily because of their social status, popularity, connections, or online following. Unlike traditional relationships driven by financial security, the attraction here is often centered on influence and visibility.
For influencers and people building personal brands, a high-profile relationship can potentially provide social capital as well as romantic attention.
Taken together, these trends point to a broader change in modern dating. Singles are not necessarily abandoning romance; they are becoming more conscious about how they approach it.
Political compatibility, emotional awareness, direct communication, and personal boundaries are playing larger roles, while dating apps are no longer the only route to meeting someone.
At the same time, trends such as shrecking and throning show that social status, appearance, and online influence can still complicate relationships.
Ultimately, the dating landscape in 2026 is less about following one universal formula and more about knowing what you want—and being honest about it.

item.title: Love, loyalty and soulmates: Young social activist Shahi Al Sadat opens up
item.description:
For Shahi Al Sadat, love is not simply about finding someone to share life with—it is about finding someone with whom life feels a little more meaningful.
In a conversation about love, commitment and soulmates, the young social entrepreneur reflects on emotional safety, loyalty, personal growth and why some people eventually become ‘home’.
What does love mean to you beyond the usual romantic definition?
For me, love is much deeper than simply having someone in your life. It is about understanding a person, respecting who they are and supporting the dreams they carry. I think genuine love should give you a sense of peace and safety. You should feel that you can be completely yourself around that person without having to pretend.
Do you believe in the idea of a soulmate?
Yes, I do. But I don't think a soulmate is someone who is simply perfect for you. I think a soulmate is someone with whom you can grow. Someone who can understand your strengths and weaknesses, communicate with you, challenge you in a healthy way and still choose to stay beside you.
A soulmate, to me, is less about perfection and more about connection.
What makes someone feel like ‘home’?
When you don't have to explain every part of yourself to them. You can talk about your ambitions, your fears, your failures or even remain silent, and they still understand you.
Some people enter your life as strangers, become important to you, and eventually become the person you feel most comfortable returning to. That's when someone starts feeling like home.
How important is loyalty in love?
Loyalty is one of the foundations of any meaningful relationship. But I don't see loyalty as controlling another person or limiting their freedom. For me, loyalty means honesty, consistency and respecting the person you've chosen.
If you genuinely care about someone, you should want to protect the trust between you—not because you are forced to, but because that relationship matters to you.
Can love and ambition exist together?
Absolutely. I don't believe someone should have to choose between love and their dreams.
In fact, I think the right person can make you more motivated. Both people should have their own ambitions, identities and goals, while also encouraging each other to grow. I would never want someone beside me to lose herself just to fit into my life. I would want us to build a life where both of us can become better versions of ourselves.
What qualities would you want in a soulmate?
I wouldn't look for perfection. I would look for honesty, kindness, emotional maturity and understanding.
I would want someone who can communicate when things become difficult, someone who can celebrate my successes but also remind me to stay grounded. Most importantly, I would want someone who genuinely wants to grow with me.
Do you think love should change people?
I think love should help people grow, but it shouldn't erase who they are.
I don't want to change someone into the person I imagine them to be. I would rather understand who they already are and grow alongside them. The healthiest kind of love allows two people to remain individuals while building something together.
What does commitment mean to you?
Commitment is a choice.
Love can be an emotion, but commitment is what you do with that emotion. It means staying honest, communicating when things become difficult and making an effort to understand each other.
It isn't about promising that everything will always be perfect. It's about saying, ‘Even when things aren't perfect, I'm willing to work through them with you.’
What do you think is the most beautiful part of loving someone?
When their happiness genuinely becomes important to you.
You start celebrating their achievements as if they were your own. You want them to succeed, to reach their dreams and to become happy—even beyond what you can personally give them.
I think there is something incredibly beautiful about watching someone you love become the person they've always wanted to be.
Do you think a soulmate has to be someone who completely understands you?
Maybe not completely. I don't think any two people can understand every single thing about each other.
But they should have the willingness to understand.
Sometimes, love isn't about having all the answers. It's about being curious enough to keep learning about the person beside you.
Finally, what would you say about the person who becomes your ‘home’?
I would say, value them.
If someone becomes your peace in a world that constantly demands something from you, that's special. If someone believes in you when you struggle to believe in yourself, that's something you shouldn't take for granted.
Some people come into your life as people. But with time, trust and love, some of them become home.
And perhaps that is what Shahi Al Sadat believes a soulmate truly is—not someone who completes you, but someone with whom you can build a life where both people feel complete in themselves.

item.title: A-Beauty brings simpler approach to skincare
item.description:
Skincare routines often involve multiple products, including cleansers, toners, essences, serums, moisturizers, and sheet masks. While South Korea’s K-Beauty popularized elaborate routines worldwide, Japan’s J-Beauty also introduced its own approach.
A different philosophy is now gaining attention in the beauty industry: A-Beauty, an Australian approach that emphasizes using fewer products to meet essential skincare needs.
The concept is simple. Instead of using numerous products for different steps, A-Beauty encourages choosing a small number of products that serve essential or multiple functions.
The approach is closely associated with Australia’s outdoor lifestyle, where exposure to sunlight, beaches, and an active way of life has influenced beauty practices.
Rather than following lengthy routines, A-Beauty focuses on using a few products according to the skin’s needs. A moisturizer, for example, may provide sufficient hydration without requiring several additional products.
This approach can save time while reducing the complexity of using multiple skincare products.
A-Beauty also draws on ingredients associated with Australia, including Kakadu plum, tea tree oil, finger lime, eucalyptus, and Tasmanian pepperberry.
Kakadu plum is known for its high vitamin C content, while tea tree oil is widely used in skincare. Finger lime, which contains naturally occurring fruit acids, is also used in some skincare products.
However, A-Beauty does not rely solely on natural ingredients. Modern skincare ingredients such as hydroxypinacolone retinoate (HPR), peptides, and ectoin are also used in products associated with the trend.
Sun protection is another key element of A-Beauty, reflecting the importance of protection from intense sunlight in Australia.
The approach emphasizes daily use of sunscreen with a sun protection factor (SPF) of 30 or higher. Reapplication is also recommended when spending extended periods outdoors.
A-Beauty moves away from the idea that skincare requires lengthy routines involving multiple products. Instead, it emphasizes understanding the skin’s needs, using a limited number of effective products and protecting the skin from ultraviolet radiation.
Foreign skincare trends are already popular in Bangladesh, with K-Beauty and J-Beauty products widely available. Interest in simpler routines is also growing as people look for skincare practices that fit into busy lifestyles.
Bangladesh’s hot and humid climate and frequent outdoor exposure can make lengthy skincare routines difficult to maintain. In this context, A-Beauty’s focus on fewer products may offer a practical approach.
A basic routine centered on essentials such as a cleanser, moisturizer, and sunscreen can be adapted according to individual skin type and needs. However, Australia and Bangladesh have different climates, so skincare practices should not be adopted blindly.
Beauty trends will continue to change, but understanding individual skin needs and choosing appropriate products remain central to an effective skincare routine.

item.title: DCCI launches week-long trade licence renewal service
item.description:
The Dhaka Chamber of Commerce & Industry (DCCI) and the Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) have jointly launched a week-long special service booth to streamline the trade licence renewal process for businesses under DSCC jurisdiction.
Simultaneously, a view-exchange meeting addressing business environment, law and order, and traffic congestion was held by the two organizations.
DSCC Administrator Md Abdus Salam inaugurated the event on Sunday (16 August) at the DCCI Auditorium in Motijheel, Dhaka.
Special guests included DSCC CEO Md Khayrul Rahman and Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) Additional Commissioner (Administration) Md Masud Karim.
The service will run from 16 August to 20 August, operational daily from 10:00 AM to 4:00 PM.
DCCI member firms and other area businesses can pay the prescribed fees on-site to renew their trade licences for FY27.
DCCI president Taskeen Ahmed stated that a trade licence is a foundational business document. However, entrepreneurs frequently encounter delays and harassment due to vague documentation rules, multiple office visits, and administrative hurdles.
He stressed that eliminating procedural delays and harassment is essential for a business-friendly environment, urging the implementation of digital solutions and multi-year trade licence renewal options.
Chief guest Md Abdus Salam highlighted that public hearings are being hosted every Saturday to ensure accountability within the city corporation, encouraging residents and business owners to participate.
Regarding fees, he noted that if the National Board of Revenue (NBR) charges levied alongside the standard trade licence fee can be reduced, the total renewal cost would drop further.
The administrator noted that while DSCC currently accounts for roughly 250,000 active trade licences, the actual number of operating commercial entities is far higher. He urged unlicensed units to legalize their operations through new registrations or timely renewals.
To ensure hassle-free public service delivery, DSCC is prioritizing digital solutions, including a proposed one-stop service mechanism.
DSCC CEO Md Khayrul Rahman reported that approximately 246,180 trade licences have been issued across 294 business categories under DSCC jurisdiction.
The revenue target for FY27 is set at Tk150 crore, seeking community cooperation to achieve it.
DMP Additional Commissioner Md Masud Karim affirmed that economic activity stalls without stable law and order, assuring that DMP gives highest priority to maintaining a safe business ecosystem.
He urged traders to report any law enforcement harassment occurring during goods unloading from trucks and covered vans in Old Dhaka.
The speakers emphasized that without reducing operational bottlenecks, expanding trade and employment remains difficult, calling for transparent, tech-driven civic services.
At the conclusion of the event, DSCC Administrator Md Abdus Salam formally handed over renewed trade licence documents to representatives of 10 DCCI member companies.

item.title: CPD: High taxes, tight credit stall RMG decarbonization push
item.description:
To maintain the global competitiveness of Bangladesh’s ready-made garment (RMG) sector, transitioning toward eco-friendly green manufacturing by reducing carbon emissions is indispensable.
International buyers are no longer prioritizing product quality and price alone; they are increasingly evaluating manufacturing processes and their associated carbon footprints. Consequently, boosting renewable energy adoption and improving energy efficiency across garment units has become critical.
However, high taxes and tariffs, elevated bank interest rates, bureaucratic delays, and limited availability of requisite technologies stand as major obstacles to this transition.
While the government claims duty-free benefits on renewable energy equipment, entrepreneurs report facing hefty tax burdens in practice. Stakeholders alleged that over a hundred containers filled with solar panels currently remain stranded at port as a result.
These observations were shared on Sunday (16 August) during a dialogue titled "Decarbonizing the RMG Industry: Challenges and the Way Forward," organized by the Center for Policy Dialogue (CPD) at the Brac Centre Inn auditorium in Mohakhali, Dhaka.
Moderated by CPD research director Khondaker Golam Moazzem, the event brought together RMG entrepreneurs, technology experts, institutional financiers, researchers, and trade body representatives.
Presenting findings from a CPD study covering 350 apparel factories, CPD program associate Sami Mohammad highlighted that meeting 30% of a factory's total electricity demand through renewable energy could reduce average monthly energy expenditure by 15.7%.
Even a 10% solar share could lower monthly energy costs by 5.5%.
Mohammad noted that over-reliance on imported LNG and other fossil fuels escalates production costs while heightening supply vulnerability. Simultaneously, pressures from international brands for sustainable manufacturing are mounting rapidly, making now the opportune time to accelerate the transition to renewables.
He added that while many garment units have taken preliminary steps to curb emissions, structural transformation lags behind—particularly in small and medium enterprises (SMEs), which face severe shortages of modern, energy-efficient machinery.
Tax burdens questioned
BGMEA vice president Barrister Vidiya Amrit Khan emphasized that European Union initiatives like the 'Green Deal' and 'Digital Product Passport' present substantial compliance challenges for Bangladeshi apparel exporters.
She warned that failing to implement proactive emission-reduction measures risks diminishing Bangladesh's market share, particularly as regional competitors like Vietnam and Pakistan outstrip Bangladesh in renewable energy adoption.
Meanwhile, local importers face steep customs duties and VAT on solar and renewable equipment.
BSREA president DM Mostafa Al Mahmud stated that despite budget speeches promising duty-free facilities for solar panels, importers encounter multiple tax levies at ports. More than a hundred solar panel containers currently remain stuck, causing factory owners to incur heavy demurrage fines.
He stressed that achieving renewable energy targets remains difficult under such conditions and called for simplifying the licensing process for merchant power plants dedicated to industrial units.
Delays in net metering
Participants pointed out that administrative bottlenecks pose as significant a barrier as capital and technology deficits.
A key grievance raised was the absence of net metering facilities in economic zones. Entrepreneurs alleged that net metering approvals, which should take 15 to 20 days, often drag on for up to six months due to red tape.
Furthermore, solar power cannot immediately replace gas or coal in heat-intensive operations such as washing and dyeing. High capital costs for industrial electric boilers deter entrepreneurs from undertaking such high-risk investments.
BKMEA executive president Fazlee Shamim Ehsan noted that while green financing frameworks exist, accessing them is overly complex. Bank interest rates hovering around 14%-15% make borrowing unsustainable for SMEs.
He added that processing loans through institutions like Idcol involves protracted delays, preventing swift investments in green technology.
He proposed establishing centralized boiler and energy distribution systems in new industrial zones to lower capital expenditure and curb emissions.
Idcol senior assistant vice president Asif Shahriar assured that efforts are underway to structure dedicated credit lines for smaller factories.
However, loan disbursements face delays due to weak financial standing or lack of repayment guarantees—an area where trade bodies like BGMEA or BKMEA could assist by providing institutional guarantees.
Discussants emphasized that while global brands demand carbon reduction, they contribute inadequately to the necessary capital investments, leaving factory owners to bear the financial burden alone.
While large factory groups maintain some capacity to self-fund tech upgrades, SMEs remain constrained by technical knowledge gaps, lack of capital, and high borrowing costs, threatening their long-term market viability.
Proposal for high-level steering committee
CPD research director Khondaker Golam Moazzem proposed forming an inter-ministerial task force under the Prime Minister's Office, comprising representatives from the Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resources, Ministry of Finance, National Board of Revenue (NBR), and business leaders.
He advocated for expedited decision-making to streamline tax, tariff, financing, and energy policies.
Moazzem added that Bangladesh's energy supply issues are unlikely to be fully resolved within the next decade, making it imperative for factories to secure localized renewable energy sources based on their operational capacity.

item.title: EWU hosts seminar on research and higher education opportunities in Japan
item.description:
The Department of English at East West University (EWU), in association with the Japanese Universities Alumni Association in Bangladesh (JUAAB), organized a seminar titled “Unlock Your Global Future: Research & Study in Japan” on Sunday, August 16, at the Manzur Elahi Auditorium of EWU.
Prof Mohammed Farashuddin, chairperson of the board of trustees of East West University, attended the seminar as chief guest.
ATM Zafrul Azam, president of JUAAB, was special guest, while Prof Sheikh Mohammad Fazle Akbar attended as guest of honor.
Prof Shams Rahman, vice chancellor of EWU, chaired the seminar.
A distinguished delegation of Japanese academics and education professionals delivered presentations during the technical sessions.
The speakers included Prof Shinjiro Ogita, dean, Prefectural University of Hiroshima; Prof Hiroki Hamada, director, Okayama University of Science; associate professor Miwa Abe and visiting professor Yoshio Maeda of Tokai University; Prof Daizo Kudo of Naase Viita Co Ltd; and Kamamoto, director of Study Japan.
The speakers discussed contemporary research trends, English-taught degree programs, Japanese language preparation, the process of identifying and communicating with potential university supervisors, and opportunities available to international students in Japan.
They also provided practical guidance on pursuing Master’s and PhD programs, developing research proposals, and preparing for academic careers and employment opportunities in Japan.
The open discussion and question-and-answer session provided students and faculty members with an opportunity to directly interact with the visiting Japanese academics and education experts.

item.title: Actress Antara arrested
item.description:
An Indian model and actress named Antara Bandyopadhyay has been arrested by India’s Railway Police for allegedly assaulting Railway Protection Force (RPF) personnel following an argument over a reserved seat on a train in Mumbai.

Antara is accused of boarding a reserved air-conditioned coach of the Aravali Express on 12 August and getting into an argument with RPF personnel. When the situation escalated, she was allegedly accused of removing her clothes and attacking the personnel with a blade.

According to reports by West Bengal-based media outlets Anandabazar and Ei Samay, the Bengali actress was travelling to Surat for a shooting assignment. She had a sleeper-class ticket. Despite having that ticket, she allegedly boarded a reserved AC coach of the Aravali Express.

The incident took place between around 9:30 pm and 10:50 pm in an area between Borivali and Dahanu.

According to the FIR filed against the actress, a passenger asked Antara to vacate the reserved seat. When she refused, the passenger informed the relevant authorities and the RPF.

RPF assistant sub-inspector Yaminikanta Mishra and constable Rajesh Kumar went to the scene and tried to bring the situation under control. Antara allegedly behaved badly with them.

Police claim that at one point the actress removed her clothes and began threatening RPF personnel with a razor blade. She allegedly also injured one of the personnel with the blade. The actress herself was injured in the incident.

According to Yaminikanta Mishra’s complaint, Antara also damaged his uniform and mobile phone.

item.title: Bobby Hajjaj: Primary education system to see major changes in 2-3 years
item.description:
State Minister for Primary and Mass Education Bobby Hajjaj on Sunday expressed hope that major and visible changes will be made to the country’s primary education system over the next two to three years.
He made the remarks while speaking to reporters after a training workshop titled “Classroom Management, Monitoring, Accountability and Changing Expectations for Local Administration in Primary Education” at the National Academy for Primary Education (NAPE) auditorium in Mymensingh in Sunday afternoon.
The workshop was organized by the Divisional Primary Education Office, Mymensingh.
The state minister said the authorities are working in a planned manner to fulfil the responsibility entrusted by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to transform primary education.
He said the workshop discussed school management, ensuring students’ rights and facilities, greater community involvement in schools and effective leadership in the education sector.
Bobby Hajjaj said the primary education sector has made significant progress during the government’s first 180 days.
He said emphasis is being placed on curriculum development, teacher training, a new teacher policy, value-based education, cultural activities, sports and technology-based learning.
Citing the prime minister’s instruction that no child should be left out of the classroom, the state minister said initiatives have been taken to provide primary students with nutritious midday meals, free uniforms, shoes and school bags to achieve this goal.
On infrastructure, he said the government’s aim is not simply to construct school buildings but to create modern, safe and student-friendly learning environments.
“We want to turn government primary schools into shining stars in every locality,” he said.
Bobby Hajjaj said a speaking test will be introduced alongside the written English examination under the new primary education curriculum to improve students’ communication skills.
He said an integrated IT ecosystem is being developed to modernize student information management and education programs, with each student receiving a unique identity.
The workshop was presided over by Divisional Deputy Director of Primary Education Md Rafiqul Islam Talukder.

item.title: HC orders halt to illegal sand extraction from Tentulia River
item.description:
The High Court has issued a rule and ordered an immediate halt to all illegal sand extraction from erosion-prone areas of the Tentulia River in Bauphal, Patuakhali.
A bench comprising Justice Ahmed Sohel and Justice Iftekhar Uddin Mahmud passed the order on Sunday after hearing a writ petition.
The court also issued a rule asking why the authorities’ failure and inaction in preventing illegal sand extraction from the erosion-affected areas of the river should not be declared unlawful.
It also sought an explanation as to why sand-mining notices issued without a hydrographic survey, in violation of Section 9(1)(b) of the Balumahal and Soil Management Act, 2010, should not be declared without legal authority.
The court ordered that all illegal sand extraction in the erosion-prone areas remain suspended until disposal of the rule.
The High Court also directed the authorities to correct records in government offices where the area has been recorded under incorrect or outdated names, such as the “Bura Gauranga” River, and identify it by its proper name, the Tentulia River.
It ordered the formation of a committee to take necessary steps in this regard and submit a report to the court within 60 days.
Advocate Muzahedul Islam Shahin appeared for the writ petitioner.
The writ petition named the secretaries of the ministries of Land and Water Resources, the BIWTA chairman, the divisional commissioner of Barisal, the deputy commissioner of Patuakhali, the Bauphal upazila nirbahi officer, the assistant commissioner (land), the officer-in-charge of Bauphal police station and the BIWTA deputy director in Patuakhali as respondents.

Garment worker killed in Sadarghat clash
item.description:
A 20-year-old garment worker was killed in a clash between two groups in Sadarghat area of Old Dhaka on Saturday night.
The deceased was identified as Mitul. Several others were injured in the incident, while police detained 10 people in connection with the clash.
Mitul worked at a garment factory in the area.
Local sources said members of the local Swechchhasebak Dal brought out a protest procession later that night following Mitul’s death. During the procession, they chanted slogans against several Jubo Dal leaders.
Sources said former Jubo Dal leader Sobhan and Kiran, senior joint convener of Dhaka South Metropolitan Chhatra Dal, are known as followers of Mohammad Suman Bhuiyan, convener of Dhaka South Metropolitan Sramik Dal. Both are also seeking posts in the Kotwali thana unit of Jubo Dal.
According to witnesses, the 2 groups had been at odds for a long time, with the dispute allegedly stemming from the sharing of extortion money.
However, police said the clash stemmed from a longstanding dispute among workers at several small garment factories operating inside East Bengal Market in Sadarghat.
Police said the workers had been involved in a dispute for several days and that the 2 groups had clashed last Thursday. The dispute escalated again at around 8:30pm on Saturday when the groups attacked and counter-attacked each other inside the 15-storey market.
During the clash, several people, including Mitul, were injured by blows from fabric-cutting scissors. They were taken to Sir Salimullah Medical College and Mitford Hospital, where doctors declared Mitul dead.
Mitul was reportedly a member of the Swechchhasebak Dal unit in Ward 37 under Kotwali police station. He was the son of Mohammad Russell Sardar of Sahabangol village in Jhalakathi.
Asked whether he knew Mitul, Suman Bhuiyan, president of Dhaka South Metropolitan Sramik Dal, said: “I have no political relationship with them. They work as tailors, and this is their personal dispute. I do not know them personally.”
Asked whether extortion was linked to the killing, Dhaka Metropolitan Police Lalbagh Division Deputy Commissioner Muhammad Talebur Rahman told Dhaka Tribune that the incident was primarily the result of previous enmity among the workers.
“The investigation is still underway. We detained 10 people last night. CCTV footage has also been collected from the scene and surrounding areas,” he said.

Renaissance paintings stolen from Italian museum
item.description:
Four works “of extraordinary value” by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina have been stolen from a museum in Sicily, Italy’s culture ministry said Sunday.
The theft, which includes three panels of the 15th-century San Gregorio Polyptych, occurred late Saturday at a museum in Messina, the religious painter’s hometown.
The theft comes just months after the Italian state bought a work called “Ecce Homo” by Antonello da Messina at a New York auction in New York for nearly 13 million euros.
Messina mayor Federico Basile called the theft “deeply reprehensible," saying it was “even more painful” as it took place during traditional city celebrations in honor of the Virgin Mary.
Art thefts are frequent in Italy.
Italian police two days ago said they had recovered three paintings by Renoir, Cézanne, and Matisse worth over nine million euros that had been stolen from a museum near Parma in northern Italy in March, allegedly by a gang of Moldovans.

item.title: More than 700 humanitarian aid trucks enter Afghanistan from Pakistan
item.description:
More than 700 trucks carrying international humanitarian aid arrived in Afghanistan via Pakistan despite a near-total closure of the land border between the two countries following clashes in October, the United Nations said Sunday.
The convoy was carrying “food and other critical humanitarian items,” Olga Cherevko, spokeswoman for the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) in Afghanistan, told AFP.
United Nations Resident & Humanitarian Coordinator for Pakistan Mo Yahya said on X that “seven hundred and twenty-four trucks of humanitarian cargo have crossed into Afghanistan through Torkham, reaching families who need it most."
He also thanked Islamabad and “all those who made it possible to keep the humanitarian lifeline open."
Acute child malnutrition has reached critical levels in Afghanistan this year, the World Food Program (WFP) warned in early August.
Following deadly earthquakes last year, several climate-related disasters this year, and the return of millions of Afghans from Iran and Pakistan since 2023, nearly 14 million Afghans are facing acute hunger, according to WFP.
The conflict with Pakistan, which has led to the near-total closure of the land border between the two countries since October 2025, has severely disrupted logistical routes for delivering humanitarian aid, WFP Deputy Executive Director Carl Skau told AFP in May.
Fortified biscuits destined for Afghan schoolchildren that were arriving from Pakistan earlier this year had to be rerouted through Iran before the war there also disrupted that route.
The biscuits eventually reached Afghanistan months later after a land and sea journey passing through countries including Jordan, Turkey, and Azerbaijan.

item.title: Israel vows to go after Hezbollah as it names another killed
item.description:
Israel vowed Sunday it would hit Hezbollah again if threatened, as it identified what it described as a commander killed in strikes a day earlier that also left several children dead.
Israeli strikes on Saturday killed 11 people in southern Lebanon, according to authorities, in the deadliest attacks since a deal was reached in June aimed at ending hostilities.
Israel said the strikes were a response to Hezbollah setting off explosive drones inside a so-called “security zone” in southern Lebanon, seriously injuring three Israeli troops, including an officer.
“No score will be left unsettled in any arena. We’ll defend our soldiers and our civilians with full power,” Defense Minister Israel Katz wrote on X.
The Israeli military identified one of those killed on Saturday as Abu Hassan Alaa, saying he was a senior commander of Hezbollah’s Badr unit who had been involved in firing drones at Israeli troops.
Israel earlier said that the strike killed a commander in Hezbollah’s elite Radwan Force, Ali Samir Al-Haj Hassan.
The Israeli military acknowledged that Hassan’s family was present but defended the strike by saying they were not the target.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said a “whole family” had been killed in the strike in the village of Ansar, with Lebanon’s health ministry reporting that three children and two women died.
Imran Riza, the UN humanitarian coordinator for Lebanon, condemned the strike.
“Children and civilians continue to pay an unacceptable price. International humanitarian law is clear: civilians must be protected at all times,” he said.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office accused Hezbollah of deliberately placing civilians in harm’s way.
Hezbollah denied the account, saying that “another entire family has been wiped out following orders issued by Netanyahu."
“Netanyahu, who is the subject of proceedings before the International Criminal Court over war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza, is once again presiding over the killing of Lebanese civilians,” Hezbollah said in a statement.
Hezbollah pulled Lebanon into the regional war in March by firing rockets at Israel in support of Iran, after US-Israeli strikes that sparked war in late February.
Lebanon and Israel signed a US-brokered deal in which Lebanon’s army will gradually take over security in southern areas occupied by Israel, but Hezbollah has refused to disarm.

item.description:

RAB-2 Commander Naimul Hasan disclosed the matter at a press briefing at the unit’s Mohammadpur headquarters.

The raid yielded a foreign-made 7.65mm pistol, a magazine, a locally made revolver, two rounds of ammunition, 260 grammes of gunpowder and two samurai swords, RAB said.
Naimul Hasan said several cases had previously been filed against Shahrukh with Mohammadpur Police Station, including two for theft, attempted robbery, attempted murder and intimidation; one for murder; one under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act; and one under the Speedy Trial Act.
Tarekuzzaman Tarek also has a case filed with Mohammadpur Police Station on charges of theft, attempted murder and intimidation, RAB said.

item.title: Nitai Roy: Govt working for proper management of water resources
item.description:
Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury on Sunday said Bangladeshis are known as a nation of “fish and rice” and the country is one of the best in the world in terms of natural resources and scenic beauty.
“The government is working to advance the country through proper management of water resources and development of canals and wetlands,” he said while speaking as the chief guest at the inauguration ceremony of National Fisheries Week being observed under the theme “A self-reliant country through silver fish, Bangladesh first.”
Jointly organized by Department of Fisheries (DoF) and Khulna District Administration, the minister attended the discussion and award-giving ceremony as the chief guest at the conference room of Khulna Deputy Commissioner’s office.
Despite facing drought, floods, excessive rainfall and other natural adversities, Bangladesh produces a huge quantity of fruits and crops, he said.
The minister also called upon farmers, blacksmiths, potters, weavers, fishermen and people from all walks of life to work together to achieve self-sufficiency in every sector.
“Imports must be reduced by increasing domestic production. In particular, we can meet the country’s demand for fish and also earn foreign currency by exporting fish after increasing production,” he said.
Nitai Roy Chowdhury urged all to move forward united with dreams, hopes and aspirations and build a prosperous, self-reliant and developed Bangladesh through collective efforts.

item.title: Noise pollution reaches alarming levels in Rajshahi
item.description:
Noise pollution in Rajshahi city has reached an alarming level, with recent measurements showing average peak noise levels above 100 decibels at two major locations, raising fresh concerns about public health, traffic management and urban environment.
A survey conducted at Railgate and Laxmipur intersection on Saturday showed average peak noise levels of 101.5 and 102.6 decibels respectively. The monitoring was conducted by Barendra Environment Development Organisation with support from Barind Environment.
The organisation has been measuring noise levels at key points across Rajshahi since 2022, following similar locations and time schedules to track changes. This year's measurements were conducted during the city's busiest hours.
At Railgate, measurements taken from 10:00 am to 10:30 am recorded an average peak level of 101.5 decibels. At Laxmipur Intersection, the level reached 102.6 decibels between 10:30 am and 11:00 am. Last year, the average peak level at both locations was around 97 decibels, indicating a significant increase within a year.
A 2022 United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) report identified Dhaka as the world's noisiest city and Rajshahi as the fourth-noisiest, recording Rajshahi's noise level at around 103 decibels.
Under Bangladesh's Noise Pollution (Control) Rules, 2025, areas are classified as silent, residential, mixed, commercial and industrial zones. During the daytime, the permissible noise level is 70 decibels in commercial areas and 50 decibels in silent zones.
Railgate is a commercial area, while Laxmipur Intersection has the characteristics of a silent zone because several government and private hospitals are located there. The recorded levels were therefore far above the applicable legal limits.
Field observations found large numbers of battery-run three-wheelers and auto-rickshaws at both locations. Many were fitted with high-volume horns, while drivers frequently honked without apparent necessity. Buses at Railgate were also observed using their horns unnecessarily.
The organisation identified haphazard bus stops, unregulated movement of auto-rickshaws and rickshaws, and poor lane management as factors contributing to excessive honking.
It recommended banning high-volume horns, ensuring approved horns on battery-run vehicles, introducing designated lanes for rickshaws and auto-rickshaws, and preventing buses from stopping outside designated points.
It also called for reasonable speed limits and effective enforcement on city roads. Better traffic management, it said, could reduce sudden braking, rapid acceleration and unnecessary honking.
Prolonged exposure to excessive noise can damage hearing and contribute to irritation, sleep disturbance, high blood pressure and cardiovascular problems. It can also adversely affect birds, animals and urban biodiversity.
The organisation urged the Rajshahi City Corporation, law enforcement agencies, transport authorities, drivers and residents to work together to control noise pollution. It particularly called for strict enforcement of a “No Unnecessary Honking” policy around hospitals, educational institutions and densely populated areas.

item.title: Power outages disrupt tea production in Moulvibazar
item.description:
Severe load shedding amid the ongoing heatwave is disrupting tea processing and production across Moulvibazar, raising concerns over production targets, rising costs and the quality of tea.
The district is home to 93 tea gardens, many of which are experiencing prolonged power outages during the peak tea-producing season. The frequent interruptions have severely hampered factory operations, while the use of generators to keep processing units running has significantly increased production costs.
Tea industry officials said frequent power cuts and fluctuations are also damaging expensive machinery and disrupting critical stages of tea processing.
Tahsin Ahmed Chowdhury, chief operating officer of Finlay Tea Company in Sreemangal, and GM Shibli, chairman of the Sylhet branch of the Bangladesh Tea Association, expressed serious concerns over maintaining tea quality and meeting production targets.
They said uninterrupted electricity is essential for every stage of processing, including drying freshly plucked leaves at the required temperature, rolling and crushing the leaves, and the oxidation process.
“Delays in processing the leaves at the appropriate time are affecting the quality of tea,” they said.
The prolonged outages, both during the day and at night, are also disrupting education, businesses, agriculture and emergency healthcare services across the district. Children, elderly people and patients are suffering the most amid the intense heat.
Students are particularly affected by extended nighttime power cuts, which are making it difficult for them to study. Many families are also being forced to endure sleepless nights due to the heat and lack of electricity.
Bangladesh Tea Board Chairman Major General Mesbah Uddin Ahmed acknowledged that the power crisis was causing losses to tea production. He said the government was working to resolve the problem and expressed hope that the situation would improve soon.
Indrajit Debnath, superintendent engineer of the Operation and Maintenance Division of the Moulvibazar Bangladesh Power Development Board, also said the electricity crisis would be resolved soon and that the situation would not continue for long.
Moulvibazar Palli Bidyut Samity General Manager Engineer Sujit Kumar Biswas acknowledged the severe load shedding amid the heatwave.
“Due to inadequate electricity supply against demand, disruptions are occurring in power distribution to consumers. However, we hope the problem will be resolved very soon,” he said.
According to Bangladesh Tea Board data, the country has set a target of producing 104 million kg of tea in 2026.

item.title: ‘Mini Switzerland’ in Rajshahi emerges as new tourist attraction
item.description:
A newly emerged sandbar in the Padma River is attracting growing numbers of visitors after photos and videos on social media branded the scenic spot as Rajshahi’s "Mini Switzerland".
Located in Char Khidirpur area of Paba upazila, the sandbar is locally known as Middle Char. Its white sand, green fields, grazing cattle, Kash flowers and vast stretches of the Padma have turned it into an emerging destination for nature lovers and day-trippers.
Visitors usually travel to the char from Dogor Ghat by boat, a journey that takes about 30 minutes, followed by a roughly two-kilometre walk to the main settlement. Boats have been carrying visitors throughout the day, and boatmen say passenger numbers have increased sharply in recent weeks.
“Just two weeks ago, boatmen used to spend their time sitting idle at this ghat. Suddenly, people started coming to visit the char,” said boatman Sujon Ali. He said the fare remains Tk25 per person and that the increased flow of visitors has improved their earnings.
Middle Char changes dramatically with the seasons. During the monsoon, the Padma surrounds the sandbar with water, while receding water reveals broad stretches of white sand. In autumn and winter, Kash flowers add colour to the landscape, while green vegetation and grazing livestock create a striking contrast.
The scenery is particularly attractive in the late afternoon, when sunlight reflects on the river and the changing colours of the sky appear on the water.
The term “Mini Switzerland” is not an official tourism designation. It is an informal nickname popularised by visitors and social media content creators. Although the char has long been familiar to local residents, Facebook, YouTube and TikTok videos have recently introduced it to people across Rajshahi and beyond.
Mohammad Mobasher, a ninth-grade student of Madinatul Ulum Kamil Madrasa, said he visited after watching videos online.
“I saw many videos about this char on Facebook and YouTube. I really like it here,” he said. “There is a huge field beside the vast river, and the whole area is green. Cattle are grazing across the field. We played football with our friends and went swimming in the river. Overall, we had a great time.”
Rajshahi College student Ishrat Jahan visited the char with seven friends. She said the open landscape offered a sense of freedom that was difficult to find in the city.
“It feels like opening a window to the outside world,” she said.
Despite the rising number of tourists, Middle Char remains home to a community dependent mainly on agriculture and livestock. Most houses are made of corrugated metal sheets and straw, while raised sandy paths serve as roads.
Livestock farming is an important source of income. Some herds contain between 80 and 300 animals, including cows, sheep, goats and buffaloes. Milk produced on the char is sold in Rajshahi city, including to hotels and other businesses, while some residents sell milk along the river embankment for Tk70-Tk80 per litre. Jute is another important seasonal activity.
However, the rising river level has disrupted daily life. Char Khidirpur Government Primary School has experienced declining attendance as students struggle to cross waterlogged areas. Teachers expect attendance to improve after the water recedes.
The growing tourist presence has also raised safety concerns, especially during the monsoon. Changing sandbanks, soft sand, sudden depressions and strong river currents can pose serious risks.
On August 13, Rajshahi City Corporation distributed life jackets to boatmen at the ghat and instructed them to prevent overloading and ensure passengers wear life jackets. Naval Police are also encouraging visitors to follow safety measures.
Local residents have urged tourists not to leave plastic, polythene or food packaging behind. Officials and community members believe Middle Char could become a significant tourism destination if its popularity is managed responsibly.
Improved boat safety, waste-management facilities, visitor guidelines and community-based tourism could help develop the char while protecting its natural environment. For now, the Padma, white sand, greenery and open sky continue to draw visitors seeking a brief escape from the bustle of Rajshahi city.
Rajshahi region Naval Police Superintendent Mohammad Billal Hossain said passengers were being encouraged to use life jackets.
“Many passengers are still reluctant to wear life jackets, but we are trying to convince everyone,” he said.
Harian Union ward member Shahidul Islam said the number of visitors had increased significantly after content creators began posting photographs and videos of Middle Char.
He urged visitors to refrain from throwing plastic, polythene and food packaging on the char.
Local residents and officials believe the area could become a significant tourism destination if the growing popularity is managed properly.

item.title: Bhashani Hall crumbles after years of neglect, restoration still uncertain
item.description:
Once the cultural heartbeat of Tangail, the historic Bhashani Hall now stands abandoned and in ruins after years of neglect, with residents alleging that the dilapidated premises have become a hub for drug users and other anti-social activities.
Cultural activists and local residents have renewed calls for the immediate restoration of the landmark auditorium, saying its prolonged closure has dealt a serious blow to the district's cultural life. Authorities, however, say renovation work will begin soon.
Located in the centre of Tangail town, Bhashani Hall served for decades as the district's premier venue for theatre, music, dance, poetry recitals, book fairs and political gatherings. However, years of poor maintenance rendered the building unsafe, prompting the administration to declare it abandoned about a decade ago.
A recent visit to the site revealed extensive deterioration. Cracks have spread across the walls, plaster has peeled away, and most rooms remain locked and unusable. Dust and debris cover the interior, while trucks are routinely parked inside the compound.
Residents said a betel leaf shop operates from the hall's veranda during the day. After sunset, they alleged, the abandoned premises become a gathering place for drug users and other anti-social elements.
"The hall has been left to decay while anti-social activities continue unchecked," said a local resident.
The foundation stone of the auditorium was laid on August 16, 1976, and it was inaugurated on April 2, 1978, using entirely local technology. Initially named Tangail Town Hall, it was later renamed Bhashani Hall in honour of veteran political leader Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani.
The nearly 1,000-seat auditorium was once regarded as the cultural centre of Tangail, hosting virtually every major cultural event in the district.
"Almost every major cultural programme in Tangail used to be held here," said renowned musician Firoz Bachchu, who attended the hall's inauguration. "Today, we have no venue capable of hosting large-scale performances."
Bangladesh Betar and Bangladesh Television artiste Masum Ferdous said many of the district's cultural organisations had gradually become inactive following the decline of the hall.
"Bhashani Hall was once the meeting place for artists and cultural organisations. Without it, cultural activities have steadily diminished," he said.
Poet Mahmud Kamal urged the government to either renovate or rebuild the auditorium, saying repeated demands for its restoration had gone unanswered for years.
Cultural organiser Harun Or Rashid said reviving the hall would not only restore Tangail's cultural heritage but also provide young people with positive recreational opportunities.
"If we want to keep young people away from drugs and juvenile crime, we need to strengthen cultural and sporting activities. A modern auditorium is essential for that," he said.
On June 12, State Minister for Fisheries and Livestock and local MP Sultan Salahuddin Tuku visited the site and assured residents that steps were being taken to restore the historic building.
"Bhashani Hall is an important part of Tangail's history and cultural identity," he said. "We have already initiated the process, and work will begin as soon as possible."
When contacted regarding the matter several times, District Commissioner Sharifa Haque could not be reached.
When contacted about the matter, Additional District Magistrate (General) Sanjay Kumar Mohanta said he was unable to comment without the district administration's permission.

BNP Senior Joint Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi on Sunday said the nation will never forget the contributions of former prime minister and BNP chairperson Begum Khaleda Zia, describing her as a towering figure who remained a source of strength and shelter for the people until her death.
“She became a towering figure to the people of this country. She provided shade to the entire nation like a giant tree until her death. Her memory will remain forever alive in our hearts,” he said.
Rizvi, who has recently been inducted into the BNP Standing Committee, made the remarks while addressing a doa and milad mahfil organized by the Bangladesh Nationalist Lawyers Forum at the Supreme Court in the capital, marking Khaleda Zia’s 81st birth anniversary.
He said Khaleda Zia endured arrests, oppression and persecution, while the government ignored her deteriorating health.
“The fascist Awami League government did not provide her with proper treatment during her imprisonment. She was also not given treatment during the 1/11 episode,” the BNP leader said.
He said BNP leaders and activists were not deterred by repression by the then government, including arrests, cases, remand and interrogation, as they drew inspiration from Khaleda Zia.
According to Rizvi, Khaleda Zia’s political career demonstrated an “extraordinary and unprecedented” consistency between her words and actions. “That is why the people never forgot her. When the first fair, free and inclusive election was held, Begum Zia emerged victorious in 1991,” he said.
He said Khaleda Zia never deviated from her commitment to the country’s independence and sovereignty, whether in government or on the streets.
Referring to the sharing of the Ganges waters, the BNP leader said Khaleda Zia had raised Bangladesh’s demand for its rightful share at the United Nations when she was prime minister.
He said Khaleda Zia introduced free education for girls up to the intermediate level and had pledged to extend the facility to the bachelor’s level if she returned to power.
Rizvi said Khaleda Zia will remain immortal in the nation’s memory for three commitments: independence and sovereignty, democracy and the rule of law.
